transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025‑12‑30 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~75m
Attendees listed above (AE+SE + CISO + Infra + Security Eng)
Materials referenced: redwood-private-vpc-reference.pdf (link), redwood-kms-byok-playbook.docx (link), Veridian SOC2 scope (internal)

00:00 Alex (AE): Hey all, thanks for joining, happy holidays everyone, we'll run through the architecture, try to keep it practical. I'm Alex from Redwood, Jordan our SE will drive the technical portion.
00:22 Priya (CISO): Thanks Alex. We wanted a focused session on network isolation and how your on‑prem pattern looks. Main concerns are egress control, key ownership, and audit evidence for SOC2.
00:34 Jordan (SE): Great, we'll do a deep dive. Quick show of hands—who runs SIEM today?
00:40 Maya (Security Eng): We push to Splunk.
00:42 Elliot (Network Ops): And we use Palo Alto for NGFW.
00:45 Jordan (SE): Perfect. I'll call out log endpoints.
---
05:12 Jordan (SE): First slide — high level options: hosted private (customer VPC peering / transit), dedicated managed in customer VPC, and on‑prem installer. The prod pattern you asked about is Held Perimeter: strict egress only to named endpoints, KMS BYOK, and no public egress from compute nodes.
05:48 Tomás (Infra): What do you mean by named endpoints? Do we have to open to Redwood's control plane IPs? We can't allow wide internet ranges.
06:04 Jordan (SE): Two approaches—route through a narrow set of egress proxies (either your NAT + proxy or Redwood managed egress endpoints in a transit VPC). For strictest control you'd proxy TLS through a verified FQDN via mTLS to an egress proxy we mutually trust. That keeps destination allow‑lists small.
06:40 Priya (CISO): We need to avoid long IP allow‑lists. FQDN + mTLS is preferable. How does that work with private deployments?
06:52 Alex (AE): For private deployments we support an egress handshake: customer runs an outbound TLS tunnel to Redwood's ingress for control‑plane (optional), or we can run a fully offline artifact model where you pull container images from an internal registry. The security doc has both patterns.
07:22 Maya (Security Eng): For audit we need full request logs — which service logs do you expose?
07:30 Jordan (SE): We expose request/response metadata, token IDs (hashed), model version, latency, per‑route errors; exports to syslog/Splunk/Datadog. Note: We don't log full PII content if you enable data masking, but audit trails include request ids and timestamps.

12:03 Elliot (Network Ops): How do you handle KV cache and state? We can't have customer data leak to shared caches.
12:15 Jordan (SE): Good question—KV cache is per‑tenant and can be pinned to private backing. For Dedicated we reserve GPU pools and memory; for Private/on‑prem the KV store is local to your cluster and never egresses. Apologies earlier slides may say K‑V cash in the auto transcript, but it's per‑tenant.

18:30 Tom Brandt (Solutions Architect): Let's talk ingress. We plan to only allow traffic from internal services into the inference cluster via a service mesh. Is there a recommended placement for NGFW vs service mesh?
18:45 Jordan (SE): Typical pattern: DMZ with ingress LB fronting a layer of proxies that terminate TLS and forward to service mesh sidecars. NGFW sits at the perimeter controlling north‑south, and host firewalls handle east‑west between zones. For on‑prem you can also install a lightweight EDR and host firewall policies.

22:10 Priya (CISO): For SOC2 evidence — we need proof of key lifecycle, rotation, and access controls. How does Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM?
22:25 Jordan (SE): We support BYOK via AWS KMS import keys or external HSMs (SafeNet/Thales). For on‑prem we can provision a KMIP bridge to your HSM; Redwood will never store plaintext keys. We surface key usage logs in the audit stream. Key rotation is controllable by your KMS policies.
22:51 Priya (CISO): Do you have an HSM attestation / FIPS guidance?
22:57 Alex (AE): Yes, our BYOK playbook references FIPS‑validated HSMs and shows how to capture attestation docs; we'll attach that.

30:05 Maya (Security Eng): How are identities and service accounts mapped? We use Okta and want SSO + SCIM provisioning.
30:19 Jordan (SE): We support SAML SSO plus SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role based and mapable to Okta groups. For service‑to‑service we recommend short‑lived mTLS certs or OIDC flows with token exchange. We also support granular route ACLs per team.
30:45 Tomás (Infra): Any risk of privilege escalation between model owners and infra operators?
30:53 Jordan (SE): We separate control plane and data plane privileges. Control plane ops (rollouts, model versioning) are scoped. For Licensed features that touch data we let customers bind keys to teams so only those teams can decrypt logs or outputs.

38:12 Elliot (Network Ops): On egress — we run a managed perimeter with strict outbound blocking. If Redwood needs to call back for metrics or telemetry, how do we minimize outbound approvals?
38:26 Alex (AE): Two patterns — push telemetry to a customer endpoint (recommended), or allow egress to specific Redwood telemetry endpoints via mTLS and mutual auth. For highest compliance we can push a small agent that forwards aggregated metrics on a schedule instead of streaming.
38:50 Priya (CISO): Retention window for logs — we have to keep certain logs for 1 year for SOC2. Can you accommodate?
39:00 Jordan (SE): Yes, we can ship raw logs to your Splunk bucket or S3 (with CMEK) and you control retention. If you prefer we can stream to your SIEM via TLS.

45:10 Maya (Security Eng): What about network zoning for models that ingest PHI? We need stronger controls.
45:21 Jordan (SE): Tagging and isolation are key: create a dedicated VPC/subnet group for PHI workloads with no public egress, stricter SGs, and dedicated compute. Use network policies and host‑based encryption. Additionally, enable request redaction or content filtering at the proxy if you need to block certain patterns.

52:05 Tom Brandt (Solutions Architect): For on‑prem air‑gapped — how do updates work? We can't allow outbound to internet.
52:15 Jordan (SE): We provide an offline artifact bundle (images + dependency archive) signed by Redwood. You pull it over an internal file transfer, validate signatures, and deploy. We recommend a bastion with strict jump host controls and a scheduled maintenance window for updates. All update actions are recorded for audit.

58:30 Priya (CISO): A very practical ask — we need a runbook showing step‑by‑step how to set up egress via NAT + proxy, and a second runbook for transit VPC egress. Can you provide both?
58:43 Jordan (SE): Yes, we'll deliver both runbooks with example SGs/IAM roles and CLI commands. Also include a small terraform snippet for a transit VPC.

64:12 Elliot (Network Ops): Are there any third‑party monitors required on our side? We run Tenable for vuln scanning — will Redwood images be scanned?
64:23 Jordan (SE): Redwood scans images with SCA and will share SBOMs. For Private/on‑prem you'll run your scanner against provided images; we include CVE reports and SBOM to help.

69:45 Priya (CISO): One more — incident response. If a suspected data exfil happens, how do we coordinate?
69:55 Alex (AE): We have an IR playbook for private deployments: immediate isolation of the compute pool, snapshot logs to a secure bucket (CMEK), joint war room with customer, and forensics access via time‑boxed role. We'll share the IR playbook with redactions.

73:00 Alex (AE): Quick recap — Jordan will send architecture diagrams and runbooks; Alex to attach KMS BYOK playbook and HSM attestation samples; Priya to confirm retention windows; schedule pilot kickoff. Any final questions?
73:18 Priya (CISO): No, thanks — that covers it.
73:25 Alex (AE): Great, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for kickoff. Happy New Year all.

End transcript.
